title: Mixture-of-Depths: Dynamically Allocating Compute in Transformers

pages.title: Spend compute where it matters
pages.subtitle: Not every token needs the whole network

blocks.html: A standard transformer spends exactly the same amount of compute on every single token. The word "the" in "the cat" gets the full stack of attention and MLP layers, and so does the final token of a hard multi-step reasoning problem. That is obviously wasteful: predicting the next token is sometimes trivial and sometimes very hard, yet the model treats both identically. This paper asks a simple question: can we let the model decide, per token and per layer, whether a token even needs to pass through that layer?

The answer is Mixture-of-Depths (MoD). At each transformer block, a small router assigns a scalar score to every token. Only the top-k highest-scoring tokens get processed by the block's attention and MLP; the rest skip the block entirely via the residual connection. Because k is fixed in advance, the total compute (FLOPs) of a forward pass is known and capped before you ever run the model — unlike earlier "early-exit" or conditional-compute schemes whose cost varies unpredictably.

Transformer-based language models spread FLOPs uniformly across input sequences. In this work we demonstrate that transformers can instead learn to dynamically allocate FLOPs (or compute) to specific positions in a sequence, optimizing the allocation along the sequence for different layers across the model depth.

The headline result: MoD models can match a vanilla transformer's final loss while using a fraction of the compute per forward pass, and because each step is cheaper they can be up to ~50% faster to step during inference. Crucially, MoD is not a smaller model — it has the same or more parameters than the baseline, it just routes most tokens around most layers.

The key engineering trick is to express the routing as a top-k selection rather than a per-token threshold. Top-k guarantees a static computation graph and a fixed tensor size, so MoD plays nicely with the batched, fixed-shape execution that makes GPUs and TPUs fast. This is what separates MoD from a long line of conditional-compute ideas that were elegant on paper but awkward on real hardware.

pages.title: Why uniform compute is the wrong default
pages.subtitle: Borrowing the routing trick from Mixture-of-Experts

blocks.html: Think about how you read. You skim filler words and slow down on the surprising, load-bearing ones. A transformer cannot do this: every token is shoved through all L layers with identical cost. The paper's premise is that the difficulty of predicting a token varies enormously across a sequence, so compute should vary too — and the model should learn where to spend it rather than being told.

MoD inherits its machinery from Mixture-of-Experts (MoE). In MoE, a router sends each token to one of several expert MLPs — it chooses which computation a token gets. MoD makes a smaller, sharper choice: there is effectively one "expert" (the normal block) and one alternative (a no-op identity), so the router decides whether a token gets computed at all in this block. Same router idea, applied along the depth of the network instead of across a bank of experts.

Suppose a sequence has S = 512 tokens. In a vanilla block, all 512 tokens go through attention and the MLP. In an MoD block with a capacity of 12.5%, the router keeps only k = 64 tokens and the other 448 slide past on the residual stream untouched. Self-attention now operates over a 64-token set instead of 512 — and since attention cost grows quadratically, that is roughly a 64× reduction in that block's attention FLOPs, plus an 8× reduction in MLP FLOPs. Stack many such blocks and the savings compound.
We use a mechanism reminiscent of Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) transformers, in which a top-k routing mechanism is used to make a static, known-in-advance compute budget.

The phrase "static, known-in-advance" is doing a lot of work. Earlier conditional-compute methods (adaptive computation time, early exit, PonderNet) let each token decide for itself how much compute it wants. That sounds ideal but produces ragged, data-dependent tensor shapes that are slow to batch and hard to train stably. MoD sidesteps this entirely: by fixing k, the shapes never change, so the speedup is real on actual accelerators.

pages.title: The MoD block: router, top-k, residual
pages.subtitle: How a token decides to skip a layer

blocks.html: Here is the mechanism for one block. Every token's hidden vector x gets a scalar router weight from a tiny learned linear projection. The block then keeps the top-k tokens by weight, processes only those through attention + MLP, and routes the rest straight through. The clever part is how the router weight feeds back into the output so that the router actually receives a gradient.

blocks.tex: x_i^{l+1} = \begin{cases} r_i^l\, f\!\left(\tilde{X}^l\right)_i + x_i^l, & \text{if } r_i^l > P_\beta\!\left(R^l\right) \\ x_i^l, & \text{if } r_i^l < P_\beta\!\left(R^l\right) \end{cases}

blocks.html: Reading it term by term. x_i^l is the hidden vector for token i at layer l, a vector in R^d where d is the model width. r_i^l = w_θ · x_i^l is the scalar router weight for that token, produced by a learned vector w_θ ∈ R^d. R^l is the set of all router weights for the sequence, and P_β(R^l) is the β-th percentile of those weights — the cutoff that selects the top-k. f(·) is the block's actual computation (self-attention then MLP), and X̃^l is the small set of selected tokens that f runs on.

The two branches say it cleanly. Top branch (token is selected): the token's new value is the block's output f(X̃)_i scaled by its own router weight r_i^l, added back to the residual x_i^l. Bottom branch (token not selected): the new value is just the old value — a pure identity skip, zero compute. The capacity β sets how many tokens survive: if β = 0.875 then 87.5% are dropped and only 12.5% are processed.

Why multiply the output by r_i^l instead of just routing? Because that scalar puts the router on the gradient path. The selected token's contribution is weighted by r_i^l, so the loss can push that weight up or down — the router learns which tokens were worth processing. The authors note this "gradients flow through the router" behavior is what lets the routing decisions improve during training rather than staying random.

Critically, the routing decision is non-trivial because the token's representation will be used by other tokens via self-attention... including the router's weight in the residual pathway means gradients pass through the routing decision, allowing it to be learned.

A subtlety the paper highlights: a skipped token is not gone. Even if token i bypasses the block, other selected tokens can still attend to its (unchanged) key and value in self-attention. So skipping a layer for a token does not isolate it — its information remains visible to the rest of the sequence. This is why routing is a genuinely hard learning problem and not just dropping tokens.

pages.title: The causal-sampling problem and how to dodge it
pages.subtitle: Top-k is non-causal, so predict the choice instead

blocks.html: Top-k has a hidden flaw for language models. To pick the top k tokens by router weight, you must compare a token against all the others in the sequence — including tokens that come after it. During training that's fine (the whole sequence is present). But at inference you generate left to right and cannot see future tokens, so you cannot know whether the current token is in the top k. This is the non-causal problem, and it must be solved or MoD would be untrainable for autoregressive sampling.

The paper tries two fixes and reports both. The first is a small auxiliary loss: a binary classifier (like the routing-balance loss in MoE) is trained to predict, from a token's hidden state alone, whether it would have been in the top k. The second, which they find simpler and reliable, is a tiny auxiliary MLP predictor — a second router that outputs a yes/no "will this token be selected" decision causally, using only information available up to the current position.
These approaches introduce no new significant computation and... allow us to sample from the MoD transformer autoregressively, while only minimally affecting performance.

The reassuring finding: the predictor only needs to be approximately right. The auxiliary methods cost almost nothing and barely dent quality — the model is robust to the occasional token being routed differently at inference than it would have been during training. So the elegant top-k training and the causal autoregressive inference can coexist.

Imagine layer 5 of an MoD model on the sentence "the capital of France is ___". The router scores each token. Filler tokens ("the", "of", "is") get low weights; the content tokens ("capital", "France") and the prediction position get high weights. With 12.5% capacity on a short sequence, only the highest-scoring positions enter the block; the filler tokens ride the residual past layer 5 untouched. The model has learned to concentrate that layer's compute on the tokens that determine the answer — exactly the behavior the routing heatmaps in the paper display.

pages.title: Free lunch on the isoFLOP frontier
pages.subtitle: Same compute, lower loss, faster steps

blocks.html: The central experiment is an isoFLOP analysis: hold the training compute budget fixed and ask whether an MoD model can match or beat a vanilla transformer trained on the same budget. The clean result is that there exist MoD configurations that are strictly better than the optimal baseline — same FLOPs, lower loss. That is the rare "free lunch": the routing doesn't just trade quality for speed, it can improve both.

There exist MoD variants that take a fraction of the FLOPs per forward pass... yet achieve lower loss than the isoFLOP optimal baseline. Some of these models step as much as 50% faster during sampling.

The winning recipe they identify: aggressive capacity (route only 12.5% of tokens) but apply MoD on alternating blocks rather than every block. Routing every other layer keeps a full-compute layer in between, which preserves enough capacity for the hard cases while still slashing total FLOPs. The best MoD variant in the search used a capacity of 12.5% with this alternating pattern.

Why does this beat the baseline rather than just matching it? Because at a fixed FLOP budget, the saved compute can be reinvested: an MoD model can be larger (more parameters / more layers) for the same per-step cost as a smaller vanilla model. More representational capacity, spent only where the router deems it useful, ends up at a lower loss. The model effectively buys depth and width by not wasting compute on easy tokens.

The speed number is the headline for deployment: because each forward step processes far fewer tokens through the expensive layers, some MoD models step up to 50% faster during autoregressive sampling. For a chatbot or any latency-bound generation workload, that is a direct, compounding win on top of equal-or-better quality.

pages.title: Learned routing, ablations, and MoDE
pages.subtitle: What the model learns, and combining with experts

blocks.html: Does the router learn something sensible, or is it routing at random? The paper checks by replacing the learned router with random (stochastic) routing at the same capacity. Learned routing wins clearly — performance is much better than dropping tokens at random — which confirms the router is identifying genuinely useful tokens rather than the savings coming "for free" from any sparsity.
Learned routing is critical: when MoD transformers use stochastic (rather than learned) routing they perform significantly worse.

The routing patterns themselves are interpretable. Across the sequence and across depth, the model concentrates compute non-uniformly, and the choices are consistent and structured, not noise. This is direct evidence that some token positions really are harder to predict and the model has discovered which ones — the original motivation, now validated empirically.

Because MoD reuses the MoE routing machinery, the two compose naturally into MoDE (Mixture-of-Depths-and-Experts). The paper describes two flavors: a staged MoDE that first applies the MoD layer-skip routing and then the MoE expert routing in sequence, and an integrated MoDE that folds the "skip this block" option into the expert router itself — adding a no-op as one of the expert choices. Integrated MoDE is the cleaner design: one router decides both whether to compute and which expert to use.

The takeaway is that MoD is an orthogonal axis of sparsity. MoE makes models sparse across width (pick a few experts); MoD makes them sparse across depth (skip layers). Stacking both lets a model be conditionally sparse in two dimensions at once, multiplying the compute savings — a natural next step for efficient large-model design.

pages.title: Why Mixture-of-Depths matters
pages.subtitle: Conditional compute that actually runs fast

blocks.html: Conditional computation — letting a network spend different effort on different inputs — is an old and seductive idea. Adaptive Computation Time (Graves, 2016), early-exit networks, PonderNet, and others all chased it. They struggled in practice because data-dependent compute breaks the fixed-shape, batched execution that modern accelerators need to go fast. The speedups were theoretical; the wall-clock often wasn't.

MoD's contribution is mostly about doing conditional compute in a hardware-friendly way. The top-k formulation gives a static computation graph with a fixed, known compute budget, so the savings show up as real speed on real chips. It reframes "how much compute does this token need" as "is this token in the top k for this layer" — a question with a fixed-size answer.

It also sits perfectly alongside Mixture-of-Experts, the dominant sparsity paradigm in frontier LLMs. MoE (Shazeer et al.; Switch Transformer) routes across width; MoD routes across depth; MoDE shows you can do both at once. That makes MoD a natural building block for the next generation of sparse, efficient models rather than a standalone curiosity.

items: Same parameter count as a vanilla transformer, but most tokens skip most layers — compute is decoupled from capacity.
FLOPs per forward pass are fixed and known in advance, because routing is top-k rather than a per-token threshold.
Best variant: ~12.5% token capacity on alternating blocks, matching or beating the isoFLOP-optimal baseline.
Up to ~50% faster autoregressive sampling steps at equal-or-better loss.
Composes with MoE into MoDE — sparsity across both depth and width.

blocks.html: The deeper message is a shift in how we think about transformer compute. The field had quietly accepted that every token pays the same price. Mixture-of-Depths shows that assumption was never necessary — a model can learn, layer by layer, which tokens are worth the full computation and which can simply be passed along. It is a small architectural change with a large conceptual payoff: compute is a resource to allocate, not a constant to pay.
